subject: chemistry

items.q: What is meant by corrosion?
items.correct: Destruction of a material by chemical reactions with substances around it
items.misconception: Damage that only metals suffer, caused by the air around them
items.why: Every worked example a student meets is a metal, and the definition is usually first met alongside rusting, so the general word gets narrowed to the one case. Read the definition as it stands: it says materials, not metals. Stonework attacked by acidic rainwater is destroyed by a chemical reaction with a substance in its environment, which fits the definition exactly.
items.random_wrong: The rusting of any metal that is left standing in air and water

items.q: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?
items.correct: Both air and water in contact with the iron
items.misconception: Water alone; the air makes no difference
items.why: Every rusty object a student has seen has been wet at some point, and air is invisible and always present, so it never registers as a variable. Water is the change they can see. A nail in water that has been boiled to remove dissolved air and sealed under a layer of oil does not rust, even though it is completely wet. The only difference from the tube that does rust is the air, so air must be necessary too.
items.random_wrong: Salt water, or water that contains an acid

items.q: Three iron nails are sealed in tubes. Tube 1: nail in tap water, open to air. Tube 2: nail in water that has been boiled, covered by a layer of oil. Tube 3: nail in dry air over anhydrous calcium chloride. Only the nail in tube 1 rusts. What does the result for tube 2 show?
items.correct: Air is necessary, since the wet nail did not rust without it
items.misconception: Water is not necessary, since this nail was wet and did not rust
items.why: Students read each tube as a separate result instead of as one variable removed from a fair test, and they focus on the unfamiliar chemical rather than on which condition it has taken away. Each tube removes one thing. The calcium chloride removes water while leaving air; no rust means water is necessary. The boiled water under oil removes air while leaving water; no rust means air is necessary. The chemicals are the method, not the explanation.
items.random_wrong: The oil layer is what stopped this nail from rusting

items.q: In the rusting experiment, why is anhydrous calcium chloride sealed in the tube with one of the nails?
items.correct: It absorbs water vapour, so the nail is left in dry air
items.misconception: It absorbs the air, so only water can reach the nail
items.why: Students read each tube as a separate result instead of as one variable removed from a fair test, and they focus on the unfamiliar chemical rather than on which condition it has taken away. Each tube removes one thing. The calcium chloride removes water while leaving air; no rust means water is necessary. The boiled water under oil removes air while leaving water; no rust means air is necessary. The chemicals are the method, not the explanation.
items.random_wrong: It coats the nail in a barrier that keeps out damp

items.q: Greasing, painting and electroplating all prevent corrosion. How do they work?
items.correct: They form a barrier that keeps air and water off the metal
items.misconception: They make the metal underneath much less reactive
items.why: Students know the coating stops the rusting and reach for a chemical explanation, treating the coating as something that alters the metal rather than something that simply gets in the way. The iron underneath is unchanged and still just as reactive. The coating only separates it from air and water. That is why a chip in the paint lets rust start immediately at that spot.
items.random_wrong: They replace an oxide layer that has flaked off the metal

items.q: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?
items.correct: An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
items.misconception: Aluminium is unreactive, so air and water do not attack it
items.why: Students judge reactivity by what they observe. Aluminium objects stay bright for years, which contradicts the reactivity series they have been taught, and the simplest way to resolve the clash is to decide aluminium is unreactive. Aluminium is reactive; it reacts quickly with oxygen. The oxide it forms stays firmly attached as a thin coating that seals the surface, so air and water cannot reach the metal below and the corrosion stops there.
items.random_wrong: Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh metal that is tougher

items.q: Iron is galvanised by coating it with which metal?
items.correct: Zinc
items.misconception: Tin
items.why: Zinc on iron is the only example students meet, and they generalise from it without checking the relative reactivity that makes the example work. Compare the two metals in the reactivity series first. Zinc above iron means zinc corrodes instead of the iron, so the protection survives a scratch. Tin below iron means a scratched tin coating leaves the exposed iron to corrode.
items.random_wrong: Chromium

items.q: Why does a zinc coating go on protecting iron even after the coating has been scratched through?
items.correct: Zinc is more reactive, so the zinc corrodes instead of iron
items.misconception: Zinc is less reactive, so air and water do not attack it
items.why: Everywhere else in the course, unreactive metals are the ones that survive, and students transfer that rule. The idea of deliberately choosing a metal that will be destroyed feels like the wrong way round. Sacrificial protection works precisely because the coating is more reactive. The zinc is attacked instead of the iron, and the iron survives while any zinc remains, which is the point of the sacrifice.
items.random_wrong: The scratch seals itself as the soft zinc spreads into it

items.q: Blocks of magnesium are bolted to the steel hull of a ship. Why does this protect the steel?
items.correct: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first
items.misconception: Magnesium is less reactive than iron, so it resists the sea
items.why: Everywhere else in the course, unreactive metals are the ones that survive, and students transfer that rule. The idea of deliberately choosing a metal that will be destroyed feels like the wrong way round. Sacrificial protection works precisely because the coating is more reactive. The zinc is attacked instead of the iron, and the iron survives while any zinc remains, which is the point of the sacrifice.
items.random_wrong: Any metal bolted to a hull will corrode before the steel does

items.q: Which statement about the metals in everyday use is correct?
items.correct: Most are alloys, which are mixtures containing a metal
items.misconception: Most are compounds, formed when metals react together
items.why: Students are taught that compounds have properties unlike their elements, and they run that rule backwards: different properties therefore compound. Alloys are also made by melting things together, which looks like a reaction. The elements in an alloy are not chemically joined in fixed proportions; they are mixed. The property change comes from atoms of different sizes disrupting the regular layers, not from a new compound being formed.
items.random_wrong: Most are pure metals, refined to remove everything else

items.q: Which statement about bronze and brass is correct?
items.correct: Bronze is copper with tin; brass is copper with zinc
items.misconception: Bronze is copper with zinc; brass is copper with tin
items.why: The two alloys are learnt together, share copper, and both have short similar names, so the second element is the only thing to remember and it is easily swapped. Pair the initials: bronze and tin both appear in bell metal for statues and bells; brass and zinc go together in trumpets and taps. Bronze - tin; brass - zinc.
items.random_wrong: Both are compounds made when copper reacts with a metal

items.q: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Which use is it best matched to?
items.correct: Musical instruments such as trumpets, and taps and fittings
items.misconception: Statues and bells, which are cast from copper and tin
items.why: The two alloys are learnt together, share copper, and both have short similar names, so the second element is the only thing to remember and it is easily swapped. Pair the initials: bronze and tin both appear in bell metal for statues and bells; brass and zinc go together in trumpets and taps. Bronze - tin; brass - zinc.
items.random_wrong: Cutting blades and tools, which must be hard and brittle

items.q: A gold ring is sold as 18 carat. What does that tell you?
items.correct: It is 75% gold, alloyed with silver, copper and zinc
items.misconception: It is 18% gold, the rest being silver and copper
items.why: Percentages are the only proportional scale most students use daily, so the number is read as one directly, without noticing that the scale tops out at 24 rather than 100. Anchor on the top of the scale: 24 carat is 100% gold. Divide by 24 and multiply by 100 for any other value, so 18 carat gives 18 divided by 24, which is 75%.
items.random_wrong: It has a mass of 18 carats, a unit used for gold

items.q: A bracelet is 12 carat gold. What percentage of it is gold?
items.why: Percentages are the only proportional scale most students use daily, so the number is read as one directly, without noticing that the scale tops out at 24 rather than 100. Anchor on the top of the scale: 24 carat is 100% gold. Divide by 24 and multiply by 100 for any other value, so 18 carat gives 18 divided by 24, which is 75%.

items.q: How do high carbon steel and low carbon steel differ?
items.correct: High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon is softer
items.misconception: High carbon steel is stronger in every way and will not break
items.why: Strong is an unambiguously positive word, while brittle and soft sound like faults. Students rank materials on a single scale of good to bad instead of matching a property to a job. Match the property to the demand. A panel must be pressed into shape without cracking, so it needs a steel that is easily shaped. Strength that comes with brittleness would make the panel crack in the press and shatter on impact.
items.random_wrong: High carbon steel is pure iron; low carbon steel is an alloy

items.q: Stainless steels are hard and resistant to corrosion. What are they?
items.correct: Iron alloyed with chromium and nickel as well as carbon
items.misconception: Iron that has been electroplated with a layer of chromium
items.why: Students have just learnt about electroplating as a barrier coating, and stainless steel looks exactly like chrome plating, so the two are merged. The chromium and nickel are part of the alloy, not a layer on it. That is why a stainless steel knife that has been ground or scratched still does not rust, unlike a plated object that has lost its coating.
items.random_wrong: A pure form of iron from which the carbon has been removed

items.q: Car body panels are pressed into shape from flat sheet. Which steel is used, and why?
items.correct: Low carbon steel, because it is softer and easily shaped
items.misconception: Stainless steel, because a chromium plating can never rust
items.why: Students have just learnt about electroplating as a barrier coating, and stainless steel looks exactly like chrome plating, so the two are merged. The chromium and nickel are part of the alloy, not a layer on it. That is why a stainless steel knife that has been ground or scratched still does not rust, unlike a plated object that has lost its coating.
items.random_wrong: High carbon steel, because it is much the strongest of them

items.q: Why are aluminium alloys, rather than steels, used for aircraft bodies?
items.correct: Aluminium alloys are low density, so the aircraft is lighter
items.misconception: Aluminium is the strongest of all the metals used in industry
items.why: Students assume the most demanding application must use the best material, and best defaults to strongest. The property that actually decides the choice, density, is not one they think of as a selling point. Steel is stronger than an aluminium alloy. Aluminium alloys are chosen because of their low density: less mass to lift means less fuel, and enough strength for the job is achieved by alloying and by the design.
items.random_wrong: Aluminium is unreactive, so the body will never need a coating

items.q: A table gives two alloys. P: density 8.9 g/cm3, very hard, corrodes in damp air. Q: density 2.7 g/cm3, moderate strength, resists corrosion. Which is the better choice for a bicycle frame kept outdoors, and why?
items.correct: Q, because it is far less dense and it resists corrosion
items.misconception: P, because the hardest alloy always makes the best frame
items.why: Students look for a single ranking of materials from best to worst, and strength is the property they can most easily interpret, so it dominates their reading of a data table. Start from what the object has to do, then read only the columns that matter to it. A frame that must be light and stay outdoors is decided by density and corrosion resistance, even if a stronger material appears in the table.
items.random_wrong: P, because a denser alloy is always the stronger of the two

items.q: Soda-lime glass is made by heating a mixture of which substances?
items.correct: Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
items.misconception: Sand, boron trioxide and limestone
items.why: Soda-lime glass is met first and becomes the default recipe, so the second glass is treated as a modification of it rather than as a different mixture. Learn them as two separate recipes. Soda-lime glass: sand, sodium carbonate, limestone. Borosilicate glass: sand and boron trioxide, and it melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
items.random_wrong: Sand, sodium chloride and limestone

items.q: Why is borosilicate glass, rather than soda-lime glass, used for laboratory glassware that is heated?
items.correct: It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass does
items.misconception: It contains limestone, which stops the glass from melting
items.why: Soda-lime glass is met first and becomes the default recipe, so the second glass is treated as a modification of it rather than as a different mixture. Learn them as two separate recipes. Soda-lime glass: sand, sodium carbonate, limestone. Borosilicate glass: sand and boron trioxide, and it melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
items.random_wrong: It is a composite, so its fibres hold the shape when hot

items.q: How are clay ceramics such as bricks and pottery made?
items.correct: Wet clay is shaped, and then heated in a furnace
items.misconception: Clay is melted and then poured into a cold metal mould
items.why: Glass and metal shaping are met alongside ceramics and both involve melting, so students generalise. The word furnace also suggests melting rather than firing. The shaping happens first, while the clay is wet and soft. The heating in the furnace then hardens the shape that has already been made. The clay is fired, not melted and poured.
items.random_wrong: Dry clay powder is pressed hard, with no heating at all

items.q: Low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. How can one monomer give two different materials?
items.correct: The two are made using different catalysts and conditions
items.misconception: The high density polymer is made from a heavier monomer
items.why: Students learn that a polymer is named after its monomer and that properties depend on the monomer, so they conclude that the monomer is the only thing that can be different. The specification says properties depend on the monomers and on the conditions under which the polymer is made. Here the monomer is the same and the conditions differ: a different catalyst and different reaction conditions give chains that pack differently, and so a different density.
items.random_wrong: The high density polymer simply has much longer chains

items.q: In terms of their structures, why do thermosetting polymers not melt when they are heated?
items.correct: Their chains are held to each other by covalent cross-links
items.misconception: Their chains are far longer and heavier than in other plastics
items.why: Students correctly learn that longer chains raise the melting point of simple molecules, then stretch that idea to explain a material that does not melt at all rather than one that melts at a higher temperature. The difference is between chains, not along them. In a thermosoftening polymer separate chains slide apart on heating. In a thermosetting polymer covalent cross-links hold the chains to one another, so no amount of heating lets them flow.
items.random_wrong: The covalent bonds along their chains are much stronger ones

items.q: A plastic saucepan handle chars but does not soften when it is heated strongly. What does this show?
items.correct: It is thermosetting, because such polymers do not melt
items.misconception: It is thermosoftening, but its chains are unusually long
items.why: Students correctly learn that longer chains raise the melting point of simple molecules, then stretch that idea to explain a material that does not melt at all rather than one that melts at a higher temperature. The difference is between chains, not along them. In a thermosoftening polymer separate chains slide apart on heating. In a thermosetting polymer covalent cross-links hold the chains to one another, so no amount of heating lets them flow.
items.random_wrong: It is thermosetting, but would melt if heated far hotter

items.q: Most composites are made of two materials. What are the two parts called?
items.correct: A matrix or binder surrounding a reinforcement
items.misconception: Two metals melted together to give a single mixture
items.why: The everyday sense of composite is simply made of parts, and students meet alloys and composites in the same topic as two kinds of mixed material. Look for the two distinct parts still present and doing different jobs: a continuous matrix, and fibres or fragments held inside it. In brass the zinc atoms are mixed among the copper atoms; there is no matrix and no reinforcement.
items.random_wrong: Fibres that surround and bind fragments of the matrix

items.q: Which of these is a composite material?
items.correct: Concrete: fragments of gravel bound by cement
items.misconception: Wool: natural fibres twisted together into yarn
items.why: Fibreglass and carbon fibre are the examples students remember, and both have fibre in the name, so fibre becomes the test instead of the two-part structure. Check for both parts. Woven cloth is fibres alone with nothing binding them. Concrete has fragments of gravel bound by a matrix of cement, so concrete is a composite and cloth is not.
items.random_wrong: Brass: copper and zinc melted to form a mixture

items.q: A table gives densities in g/cm3: steel 7.9, aluminium alloy 2.7, fibreglass 1.9, poly(ethene) 0.94. All of them are stiffer than poly(ethene). A part must be as light as possible but stiffer than a polymer. Which should be chosen?
items.correct: Fibreglass, at 1.9 g/cm3 and stiffer than the polymer
items.misconception: Steel, because at 7.9 g/cm3 the densest is always the stiffest
items.why: Heavy objects feel solid and substantial, and students merge the ideas of heavy, strong and hard into one vague notion of toughness rather than treating them as distinct measurable properties. Treat each column separately. A dense alloy can be soft, and a low density alloy can be strong enough for the job. Only the strength figures given can answer a question about strength.
items.random_wrong: Poly(ethene), because 0.94 g/cm3 is the lowest density listed

items.q: A saucepan handle must not melt, must not conduct heat well, and must be moulded cheaply in quantity. Which material is most appropriate?
items.correct: A thermosetting polymer, which does not melt when heated
items.misconception: A thermosoftening polymer, which softens only when charred
items.why: Students have met melting point as a property that every substance has, so a material that never melts does not fit their model and gets recast as one that is simply hard to melt. The cross-links between the chains are covalent and hold the whole structure together, so there is no temperature at which the chains can slide apart and flow. Heat it strongly and it chars rather than melting.
items.random_wrong: Stainless steel, the hardest and strongest of the choices

items.q: A galvanised bucket gets a deep scratch through the zinc. Will the iron now rust there?
items.correct: No. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc corrodes instead, even where the iron is exposed.
items.misconception: Galvanising is just a zinc layer, so as soon as it is scratched the iron underneath is exposed and rusts like any other bare iron.
items.why: Students have just learnt that barrier coatings fail when scratched, and they apply that rule to every coating without noticing that a reactive coating protects by a second, different mechanism. Galvanising does two jobs. It is a barrier, and it is sacrificial protection. Because zinc is the more reactive metal, it continues to corrode in preference to the iron even when the iron is exposed at a scratch.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Copper roofs turn green over time. Is that copper rusting?
items.correct: It is corrosion, but not rusting. Rusting is the name for the corrosion of iron.
items.misconception: Rusting is what all metals do when they corrode, so any corroded metal has rusted.
items.why: Rust is the only corrosion product most students can name, so the word gets used for every case of a metal being eaten away by its surroundings. Corrosion is the general term for the destruction of materials by chemical reaction with substances in the environment. Rusting is one example of corrosion, and it is specific to iron.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A ring is sold as 18 carat. Is the carat number telling you how heavy the ring is?
items.correct: For gold alloys the carat measures the proportion of gold in the alloy, on a scale where 24 carat is 100% gold.
items.misconception: Carats measure how much gold there is by mass, so a bigger, heavier ring has more carats.
items.why: Carat is also used as a unit of mass for gemstones, and advertising uses the word loosely, so students attach it to size or weight rather than to composition. Carats here are a proportion out of 24. An 18 carat ring is 75% gold whether it weighs 2 g or 20 g; only the fraction of gold is being described.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is steel a pure metal?
items.correct: No. Steels are alloys of iron that contain specific amounts of carbon and other metals.
items.misconception: Steel is what you get when you purify iron properly, so steel is basically pure iron with a different name.
items.why: Steel is presented as the better, more useful version of iron, and better is read as purer. Students also see steel treated as a single named material, which makes it sound like an element. Steel is deliberately impure: carbon is added in controlled amounts, and other metals such as chromium and nickel are added to change the properties. Different steels have different compositions, which is why they have different properties.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a thermosoftening polymer melts, what is being broken?
items.correct: The weak forces between the separate polymer chains, which lets the chains move past one another. The covalent bonds within the chains stay intact.
items.misconception: Melting a polymer breaks the covalent bonds in the chains, which is why the plastic goes runny.
items.why: Melting is described as breaking bonds in loose speech, and students do not distinguish the strong bonds along a chain from the weak forces holding neighbouring chains together. If the covalent bonds broke, the polymer would be destroyed and could not be remoulded. Thermosoftening plastics can be melted and reshaped repeatedly, which shows only the forces between chains have been overcome.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In fibreglass, which part is the matrix and which is the reinforcement?
items.correct: The resin is the matrix that surrounds and binds; the glass fibres are the reinforcement.
items.misconception: The fibres are the matrix, because they run right through the material and hold it all together.
items.why: The word matrix suggests a framework or network, and the fibres are the visible framework, so the two labels are swapped. The matrix is the continuous material that surrounds the other one. Ask which part is doing the surrounding: the resin flows around the fibres, so the resin is the matrix and the fibres are the reinforcement.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the oxide layer on aluminium flake off like rust does on iron?
items.correct: No. The aluminium oxide coating stays attached to the surface and protects the metal from further corrosion.
items.misconception: All oxide layers crumble away and expose fresh metal, so aluminium must need repainting like iron does.
items.why: Rust is the students' model of what a metal oxide does, and rust does flake away. They generalise the behaviour of one oxide to all of them. Rust flakes off, so fresh iron is exposed and corrosion continues into the metal. Aluminium oxide adheres firmly and seals the surface, so the reaction stops. The difference in behaviour of the oxide is the whole reason aluminium survives outdoors.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does iron need salt water to rust?
items.correct: No. Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust; salt is not one of the necessary conditions.
items.misconception: Rusting is caused by salt, so iron kept away from salty water or salted roads will not rust.
items.why: Students hear that salt water and gritted roads make cars rust badly, and they turn a factor that speeds rusting up into a factor that is required for it. A nail in ordinary tap water with air present rusts perfectly well, which shows salt is not necessary. Salt increases the rate of rusting; the two necessary conditions remain air and water.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
